questions.title: SECTION B (Compulsory) — Question 2: The value of work (Generation Z and the changing world of work)
questions.passageText:
THE VALUE OF WORK — Generation Z (Gen Z) and the changing world of work

Gen Z are individuals born between 1997 and 2012. Most of them are exposed to a world of widespread technology, social media and internet access.

They constantly strive for a better work-life balance and healthy relationships. They place value on the human experience, recognising that there is more to life than work. This unique perspective shapes their behaviour and the way they value work, either at school or in the workplace.

Gen Z consider transparency and openness more important than experience; they are always hungry for feedback, so much so that 73% are willing to question authority or resign if they do not receive regular feedback.

[Adapted from www.merchantcapital.co.za. Accessed on 17 July 2024.]

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term value of work. (No marks are awarded for examples.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. It could refer to the importance/worth/significance of any ONE of:
• An individual's labour or the financial worth of work that adds meaning to life / a return on investment.
• Efforts and contributions in a job/profession/career that give purpose and a sense of identity.
• Growing and developing professionally out of intrinsic motivation to work diligently.
• Work within a culture or society that influences societal norms and expectations.
• Making a positive impact in a community or society.
• Having autonomy and taking ownership of responsibilities, leading to financial independence and security.
• Self-fulfilment/happiness/purpose leading to contentment and satisfaction in a career and personal life.

questions.title: SECTION B (Compulsory) — Question 3: Study skills (Dishonesty in examinations on the increase)
questions.passageText:
STUDY SKILLS — Dishonesty in examinations on the increase

The penalties for being dishonest during matriculation examinations could include results being invalid and a postponement of the examinations that are to follow. If learners are discovered to have had access to or circulated leaked question papers, they could also face criminal charges.

It is, therefore, very important that learners understand that examination ethics, just like work ethics, means to follow the rules, guidelines and moral principles. These give direction on how assessments are conducted and the manner in which it impacts on your professional life in future. As a learner, failure to adhere to these moral principles could impact admission to higher education institutions.

Over a thousand Grade 12 learners were banned from sitting for examinations after being found guilty of cheating during the 2022 National Senior Certificate (NSC) Examinations. These learners will only be permitted to sit for the NSC examinations after the disciplinary hearings.

Grade 12 learners are obligated to sign an NSC Examination Pledge before the commencement of the final examinations as a formal commitment to upholding the values and rules of this pledge, which may motivate learners to commit to academic integrity.

[Adapted from www.iol.co.za. Accessed on 16 July 2024.]

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO actions that you may unintentionally commit in the examination room that may be considered to be dishonest. (Do not refer to bringing material or devices into the room — the focus is on actions during the sitting.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. Any TWO of:
• Making notes during reading time.
• Talking to other learners, using non-verbal gestures/body language, or turning around to ask a question during the examination.
• Borrowing, picking up or swapping stationery with other learners.
• Asking invigilators for an explanation or advice on examination instructions or questions.
• Using a smart watch, or unknowingly having a programmable calculator in the examination room.
• Peering at or constantly looking at a friend's answer script to check if you are on the same track or pace.
• Reading your questions or answers out aloud.
• Changing your handwriting style.
(2 x 1) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Why do you think some learners may feel pressurised to perform well in the NSC examinations?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• High expectations from themselves, parents, teachers, the school, the community or universities, and not wanting to disappoint these parties if they miss the standards required for financial aid or admission.
• Inadequate revision, not being prepared or not understanding content because of poor study habits or procrastination, leading to anxiety and panic as the examination nears.
• Competition within their grade and not wanting to lose their place on the top-achievers list, making them feel they must outperform others to gain higher education opportunities.
• Financial pressure within the household, leading to a strong need to provide for or take care of the family after Grade 12.
• Poor performance in their SBA throughout the year, making them desperate to improve their final results.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how dishonesty during the NSC examinations could impact on a learner's admission to higher education institutions.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• Not receiving their NSC certificate, which is crucial for admission, because their results may be cancelled or withheld.
• A disciplinary record or formal reprimand being viewed negatively by admissions officers, hindering the chances of acceptance.
• Disqualification from future examinations, leaving gaps in the academic record and making them ineligible for higher education entry.
• Suspension from the examination or school, viewed negatively when a tertiary institution considers a learner's suitability for admission.
• Loss of trust from teachers/invigilators/principal/admissions officers, making it harder to obtain positive references.
• Limited eligibility for scholarships/bursaries/financial aid/learnerships, as their academic integrity is questioned.
• Legal consequences from the Department of Education, harming their reputation and prospects under a tertiary institution's admissions policies.
• Being prevented from writing the National Benchmark Tests (NBTs) in time because of a prolonged wait for disciplinary outcomes.
• A criminal record from the dishonesty following them throughout their academic and professional journey and limiting future opportunities.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss TWO ways in which you could revise your own study strategies to ensure that you are well-prepared for the examinations.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks each for TWO well-explained responses. You could adapt your approach to learning by:
• Breaking study material into manageable parts, helping you meet your study goals.
• Assessing your current study techniques, helping you change to more effective methods.
• Identifying areas that need more focus, guiding you on how to improve in those areas.
• Considering alternative study environments so you remain focused when studying.
• Teaching or explaining the material to someone else to check your own understanding.
• Verifying your study schedule to ensure coverage of all the material.
• Considering more active learning styles, which may improve retention.
(2 x 2) (4)

subQuestions.questionText: Assess TWO ways in which honouring the NSC Examination Pledge may help you to maintain academic integrity.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks each for TWO well-explained responses. Honouring the pledge may:
• Compel you to make a personal commitment to uphold ethical standards even when stressed, binding you to the rules and standards you must follow.
• Reinforce your commitment to be true to yourself, making you more aware of the consequences of dishonesty.
• Instil a sense of accountability, since you have promised yourself, peers and teachers to uphold ethical standards, ensuring you take responsibility and preventing dishonest behaviour.
• Promote ethical decision-making when faced with academic or peer pressure to cheat, reinforcing your internal motivation to act honestly.
• Build trust between you and your peers/teachers/principal, committing you to high standards of academic conduct and encouraging peers to do the same.
• Affirm your commitment to ethical behaviour, which may influence your actions in all academic work.
• Constantly remind you of the importance of honest behaviour, deterring you from violating standards given the serious consequences.
• Encourage self-reflection, helping you align your behaviour with the values and expectations of the NSC.
(2 x 2) (4)

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse how having strong work ethics could enhance your professional skills in future. In EACH answer, also indicate how this could contribute to long-term career success.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award THREE marks each for TWO well-explained responses (statement + qualify + outcome). Strong work ethics such as:
• Responsibility and self-discipline may help you keep focus on long-term goals, and consistent performance may build a stable career path and open new opportunities.
• Collaborating with others fosters teamwork, leading to potential leadership roles.
• Adaptability in a fast-paced environment lets you thrive amid change, enabling you to take on new challenges and roles.
• Punctuality, efficiency and effective time management increase productivity and successful project completion, enhancing opportunities for future advancement.
• Integrity and accountability ensure you make appropriate choices and foster a culture of responsibility, opening doors to future career prospects.
• Being consistently professional improves your reputation in your industry, making you a preferred co-worker and candidate for promotions.
• Delivering quality work builds your reputation as a dependable employee, helping you remain competitive in your field.
• Transparency lets you build valuable, trusting relationships with mentors, possibly leading to referrals for executive or strategic positions.
(2 x 3) (6) [20]

questions.title: SECTION C (Answer any TWO of Questions 4, 5 and 6) — Question 4: The role of the media (Media coverage of sport and sports personalities)
questions.passageText:
SECTION C: Answer any TWO questions in this section. Responses must be in paragraphs; marks are awarded only for responses written in full sentences. If all three questions are answered, only the first TWO are marked.

THE ROLE OF THE MEDIA — Media coverage of sport and sports personalities

Coverage of sport and sports personalities varies in the media. Media coverage of sports personalities can lead to their fame and success. It can also draw attention to scandals, resulting in bad publicity and undue pressure on these individuals; yet these individuals may inspire young people to pursue careers in sport.

[Adapted from www.classace.io. Accessed on 17 July 2024.]

Write paragraphs on media coverage of sport using the three points below as a guideline.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly state FOUR roles of the media in promoting sports in South Africa.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. Any FOUR of:
• Educating the public about different sports, their history, rules and strategies and the importance of physical activity.
• Attracting sponsors and funding for sports teams and events and enhancing financial support for sports development.
• Increasing visibility and reaching wider audiences and spectators.
• Advertising and marketing products related to sport and sport funding.
• Shaping public opinion, perception, awareness and interest in sport.
• Challenging stereotypes related to gender/race/disability and promoting inclusivity and participation from under-represented groups.
• Highlighting health benefits, achievements and talents of athletes and teams.
• Motivating sports engagements, events and tournaments and encouraging participation, nation-building and unity.
• Creating opportunities to engage with sports personalities locally and globally on social media.
• Providing extensive coverage of sports events, competitions and athletes.
• Broadcasting live sports events in real time on designated channels.
• Providing platforms for discussion, debate and analysis of sport.
• Entertaining the public with sports events.
(4 x 1) (4)
subQuestions.topic: The role of the media in sport

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss in detail how sports personalities could potentially influence young people to consider a career in sports.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses (statement + elaborate + qualify + outcome). Sports personalities could:
• Serve as role models and share their unique stories, demonstrating values like teamwork, discipline and perseverance that are essential for success, helping the youth develop career and life goals.
• Increase awareness about various sports and careers for all genders, exposing young people to new possibilities and inspiring them to try new sports, making sports careers more appealing.
• Act as mentors through coaching clinics, providing guidance, support and skills development, building confidence within sporting codes and motivating young people to pursue related careers.
• Aspire to fame and success, which is attractive to young people who seek the same successful lifestyles and come to believe they could achieve the same status.
• Be treated like celebrities with a high level of public recognition and adoration, which the youth admire and want to achieve for themselves in sport.
• Be financially successful, which appeals to young people who want financial security, making the financial freedom associated with sports careers enticing.
• Exhibit luxurious lifestyles with access to exclusive events, travel and high-end facilities, often featured in the media, which appeals to young people who enjoy the spotlight.
(2 x 4) (8)
subQuestions.topic: The role of the media in sport

subQuestions.questionText: Examine TWO ways in which the media could report more responsibly on alleged (suspected) scandals of sports personalities.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses (statement + elaborate + qualify + outcome). The media should:
• Conduct fact-checking and verification of alleged incidents through reliable sources, so only accurate, factual information is shared with the public.
• Uphold the principle that individuals are innocent until proven guilty, presenting allegations as claims to be investigated and not delving into irrelevant aspects of a personality's life.
• Include perspectives from all sides — the accused, the accusers, legal experts and relevant institutions — as context helps the audience understand the situation better.
• Be aware of the impact of their reporting on the lives and careers of those involved, avoiding reinforcing negative perceptions or tarnishing reputations, so they do not perpetuate bias.
• Use investigative or trained journalists to ensure ethical, responsible reporting and to address conflicts of interest, privacy issues and bias, ensuring a fair and accurate report.
• Avoid sensationalism by refraining from misleading headlines, photos and posts to attract readers, maintaining a neutral tone and avoiding emotionally charged language.
• Involve athletes in their research by inviting them to share and defend their stories, presenting a more balanced view and helping the audience understand both sides.
• Adhere to professional standards by avoiding conflicts of interest and hate speech, maintaining credibility and treating the sports personality with respect and fairness.
(2 x 4) (8) [20]
subQuestions.topic: The role of the media in sport

questions.title: SECTION C (Answer any TWO of Questions 4, 5 and 6) — Question 5: Social and environmental responsibility (Participation in community service)
questions.passageText:
SOCIAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL RESPONSIBILITY — Participation in community service

Social and environmental responsibility, or community service, is the act of being accountable for one's actions and behaviour in a manner that benefits society at large. Through engaging in community service, the youth may also gain valuable employability skills.

South African youth are well aware of their social responsibility towards society and, through youth programmes, many young people are now empowered to take the initiative in making positive changes in their communities.

[Adapted from www.hmjournals.com. Accessed on 19 July 2024.]

Write paragraphs on social and environmental responsibility using the three points below as a guideline.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly state FOUR ways in which young people could promote safe and healthy living environments.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. Any FOUR of:
• Educate their peers through workshops, social media campaigns or informal discussions.
• Advocate for better policies and practices and reduce their carbon footprint within their schools and communities.
• Create or participate in safe spaces where peers can openly discuss issues.
• Actively participate in community service projects.
• Use social media platforms to share information and raise awareness.
• Join or form learner committees or clubs.
• Plan or run events like health fairs, fitness challenges or mental health workshops.
• Provide feedback to school and community leaders for improvements to current practices and programmes.
• Be role models or whistle-blowers showing personal responsibility.
• Distribute or use promotional material.
(4 x 1) (4)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss in detail how participation in community service could help the youth to improve their employability skills.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses (statement + elaborate + qualify + outcome). Community service could:
• Provide opportunities to interact with people from diverse backgrounds through inclusive community and cultural projects, teaching the importance of diversity and flexibility, which are increasingly important in a global workforce.
• Encourage the youth to take on leadership roles and plan activities, making decisions under pressure, creating a sense of accountability that makes their leadership qualities sought after by employers.
• Require public speaking, leading meetings and one-on-one conversations, helping them practise and improve verbal communication and become more articulate and confident.
• Provide opportunities to resolve disagreements and disputes by learning to compromise and mediate, finding mutually acceptable solutions important for effective conflict resolution.
• Require managing various tasks, events and meetings, helping the youth learn to prioritise and manage time and meet deadlines, developing strong organisational and time-management skills.
• Present unexpected challenges where the youth learn to think critically and creatively, becoming flexible and adaptable and more resilient to workplace change.
• Entail working with limited resources in different environments, encouraging innovative ways to achieve goals and enhancing problem-solving and analytical skills.
• Give young people work experience through volunteering that can be added to their CVs, showing they can integrate easily into the workplace.
• Provide a reliable reference from project coordinators, validating their credentials and setting them apart from other candidates.
• Provide opportunities to learn 21st-century skills, enhancing their ability to solve complex community issues and making them more valuable in the workplace.
(2 x 4) (8)

subQuestions.questionText: Examine TWO ways in which empowered young people could motivate other youth to address social issues within society.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses (statement + elaborate + qualify + outcome). Empowered young people could:
• Be peer educators, helping others understand the importance of addressing social issues and inspiring them to commit to and get actively involved in reducing social ills.
• Serve as role models and mentors by actively participating in community initiatives, showing their commitment and encouraging others to become social activists.
• Encourage other young people to initiate community projects, giving them the chance to take responsibility and fostering ownership and commitment, leading to increased youth participation.
• Form youth-led organisations that provide skills training and workshops, equipping others with practical skills, knowledge and resources to initiate sustainable projects and inspiring similar action.
• Engage other young people on social media by posting about their community work, raising awareness and encouraging others to get involved and bring about positive change.
• Share personal experiences through blogs, videos and posts, lending realism to their message about overcoming challenges and fostering a genuine desire in others to get involved.
• Establish platforms accessible to all regardless of background or skill level, so more young people can participate, discuss issues and collaborate, creating spaces that promote collective action.
• Organise online petitions, crowdfunding, campaigns or virtual events, using technology to coordinate efforts and rally support and making it easier for more people to get involved.
(2 x 4) (8) [20]

questions.title: SECTION C (Answer any TWO of Questions 4, 5 and 6) — Question 6: Lifestyle diseases (TB: a silent killer)
questions.passageText:
LIFESTYLE DISEASES — TB: a silent killer

Tuberculosis (TB) is a preventable and curable disease; yet 1,5 million people die from TB each year — making it the world's top infectious killer. Lifestyle factors and stigmatisation play a significant role in the spreading of TB in communities. In order to manage this disease effectively, early treatment is very important.

Glossary: stigmatisation — when individuals are unfairly treated and discriminated against due to conditions that are seen as undesirable in society.

[Adapted from www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis. Accessed on 16 July 2024.]

Write paragraphs on the prevention and control of lifestyle diseases such as TB using the three points below as a guideline.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly state FOUR lifestyle factors that may increase the risk of a person contracting tuberculosis. (Marks are awarded only for personal lifestyle choices, not conditions beyond a person's control.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. Any FOUR of:
• Smoking or vaping, making it easier for TB bacteria to enter the body.
• Excessive alcohol intake, reducing the body's ability to fight off TB bacteria.
• Drug use, which could weaken the immune system.
• A poor diet or poor nutrition, making it harder for the body to defend itself against TB.
• Poor personal hygiene or living unhygienically.
• Lack of physical activity or a sedentary lifestyle.
• Failing to seek medical attention for a persistent cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss.
• Living, working in or travelling to areas with high TB rates, or close contact with someone with active TB without precautions.
• Lack of sleep or chronic stress.
• Failing to regularly monitor and manage chronic conditions, compromising immune function.
• Regularly spending time in crowded social settings.
• Not using masks or other protective measures in high-risk areas.
• Not receiving or ignoring the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine.
• Constant exposure to indoor pollutants.
• Not educating yourself about TB transmission, symptoms and prevention.
• Not participating in regular health screenings.
(4 x 1) (4)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss in detail how early treatment of TB could help individuals who are infected to manage the disease more effectively.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses (statement + elaborate + qualify + outcome). Early treatment of TB could:
• Lead to shorter, less intensive treatment that is easier to complete, improving adherence and making severe complications and hospitalisation less likely.
• Prevent TB from progressing to a severe state, leading to fewer symptoms and less physical damage and a milder illness with less discomfort and fewer life-threatening complications.
• Reduce the spread of TB to others, helping the individual protect their family and community and bringing peace of mind that encourages them to stay proactive about their health.
• Produce better health outcomes, with a higher likelihood of complete recovery and a return to normal life, reducing the psychological burden of long-term health fears.
• Ensure a quicker recovery and faster reduction of symptoms like coughing, fatigue and weight loss, letting the individual return to their routine sooner and improving their independence and productivity.
• Reduce the financial burden by minimising medical expenses for prolonged treatment and lessening indirect costs such as lost wages, reducing financial stress.
• Ensure comprehensive care through regular monitoring and support, helping manage side effects and boosting the individual's confidence in their recovery.
• Reduce the risk of developing drug-resistant TB, which is harder and more expensive to treat, keeping treatment effective with fewer side effects and a higher chance of a cure.
(2 x 4) (8)

subQuestions.questionText: Examine the possible impact of stigmatisation on the effectiveness of treatment for TB infected individuals.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses (statement + elaborate + qualify + outcome). Any TWO of:
• Stigmatised individuals may be less likely to adhere to their treatment regimen because they want to avoid being seen at health facilities or taking medicine in front of others, leading them to skip doses or stop treatment, which can cause prolonged infectiousness and drug-resistant TB.
• The stress and anxiety caused by stigma may lead to mental health problems such as depression and anxiety, which interfere with the ability to follow treatment plans and reduce motivation to continue getting help.
• Stigmatised individuals may experience social isolation as they withdraw from social interaction to avoid discrimination, reducing the social support that is crucial for coping and leading to higher rates of treatment failure.
• Stigma may strain relationships with family and friends, leading to a lack of support at home as family members distance themselves out of fear of infection, negatively affecting the individual's ability to manage the disease.
• Stigmatisation may lead to workplace discrimination and job loss, causing economic hardship that makes it difficult to afford transport to health facilities or nutritious food, preventing proper care.
• Individuals who experience stigma from healthcare providers may develop mistrust, deterring them from seeking regular advice, following treatment or disclosing important information, compromising their health.
• Individuals may internalise societal stigma, leading to self-stigma and shame that diminishes self-esteem and motivation to seek or adhere to treatment, creating a sense of hopelessness.
• Stigmatisation based on cultural beliefs such as witchcraft, curses or myths may cause an individual not to seek medical help, which is detrimental to fast, effective treatment and can lead to a severe or drug-resistant strain or death.
(2 x 4) (8) [20]
